sections.h2: What a transfer on death deed is
sections.html:
A transfer on death (TOD) deed passes real estate to a named beneficiary when the owner dies, without a probate transfer for that parcel. Indiana allows it under the Transfer on Death Property Act, IC 32-17-14, with the real estate rules in section 11.

You keep the house for life. The beneficiary has no rights in the property because of the designation until you die, and if you sell, the designation ends.

The deed works when the owner, or the owner's legal representative, signs it and it is recorded with the recorder of deeds in the county where the land sits, before the owner dies.

sections.h2: What makes a TOD deed valid
sections.html:
The big requirement is recording while the owner is alive. A TOD deed that is not recorded before death is void.

  • No payment is required for the transfer.
  • The deed does not have to be delivered to the beneficiary.
  • The county auditor's endorsement is not needed to record it.
  • The beneficiary can be a revocable or an irrevocable trust.
  • The wording can be, in substance, a conveyance "TOD to" the beneficiary.

In practice, the steps are short. Confirm how title is held, have the deed prepared, sign it, and take it to the county recorder where the parcel sits. Then keep the recorded copy with your papers and tell the beneficiary where it is, even though delivery is not required. If the recorder never receives the deed before you die, it does nothing.

Since delivery is not required, a beneficiary may find out about the deed only after the owner dies. A family that suspects one exists can search the county recorder's records for the parcel.

sections.h2: How the form of ownership changes a TOD deed
sections.html:
What the deed does depends on how the owner holds title, and some forms call for extra care. Section 11 spells out the results.

Form of ownershipEffect of a TOD deed
Tenancy by the entiretyVoid unless the other spouse joins
Joint tenancy with survivorshipSevers the joint tenancy; co-owners become tenants in common
Tenancy in commonThe owner's interest passes to the beneficiary
Life estate measured by the owner's lifeThe conveyance is void

Married couples who own together should not assume one spouse can sign alone. Questions like these are a good reason to have an attorney review a recorded deed.

sections.h2: Changing or revoking a TOD deed
sections.html:
You record a later document in the county while you are alive. IC 32-17-14-16 lets the owner revoke or change the designation by recording a new deed or an acknowledged affidavit that does so. An unrecorded document is void.

Informal fixes do not work:

  • Writing on a recorded TOD deed or destroying a copy has no effect on the designation.
  • A will or trust cannot revoke or modify a TOD deed.
  • A newer designation replaces an earlier one unless it says otherwise.

For joint tenants with survivorship, a change needs the agreement of each living owner. For tenants by the entirety, both spouses must agree while both are alive.

sections.h2: Selling the house after you sign a TOD deed
sections.html:
A sale cancels the TOD for that property. Under section 16, transferring your interest during life, with or without payment, ends the beneficiary designation. A real estate deed given this way is void unless it is recorded with the county recorder before the owner dies.

So an owner with a TOD deed on record can still sell to a cash buyer. The buyer's title company searches the record, finds the TOD deed and confirms the owner's right to convey. The beneficiary has no rights in the home while the owner is alive.

Families under pressure should know this. A beneficiary cannot block a sale by the living owner, and an owner who needs to move can sell on their own schedule.

A TOD deed does not shield the house. The beneficiary takes the property subject to the liens and security interests that exist (IC 32-17-14-19). A mortgage, a recorded easement or a judgment lien stays on the house after the transfer.

Creditors keep their rights too. IC 32-17-14-29 says the chapter does not limit what an owner's creditors can do against beneficiaries and other transferees. A beneficiary's liability for creditor claims and statutory allowances is set in IC 32-17-13.

Unpaid property tax is a lien that follows the house. Our Indiana tax lien guide explains how it works. A beneficiary who inherits a house with delinquent tax inherits the tax bill with it.

sections.h2: Can a beneficiary sell after the owner dies?
sections.html:
Yes. Once the beneficiary holds title through the recorded deed, the house is theirs to sell.

A beneficiary should take these steps:

  • Get a certified death certificate.
  • Ask the title company to pull the recorded TOD deed and any later revocation.
  • Check for a mortgage, tax due or liens.
  • See an attorney if a spouse, children or other heirs may have claims. IC 32-17-14-25 covers the rights of surviving spouses and children.

A house in poor repair can still be sold as is. Cash Home Buyers makes offers on inherited Indiana homes without requiring repairs, and a cash closing skips the listing, showings and buyer financing delays.

sections.h2: Other parts of the Transfer on Death Property Act
sections.html:
The act reaches well beyond deeds. The same chapter governs designations on accounts, tangible personal property and registrations in beneficiary form, so a family may be sorting out several transfers at once.

  • Section 20 requires a beneficiary to survive the owner, and section 22 covers substitution for beneficiaries who do not survive.
  • Section 23 deals with the effect of dissolution or annulment of a marriage.
  • Section 24 deals with fraud, duress, undue influence, mistake and lack of capacity.
  • Section 17 deals with the powers of an attorney in fact, a guardian, a conservator or an agent.
  • Section 32 deals with out-of-state beneficiary designations.

Each has its own conditions. If a family member signed a deed while ill, or a divorce came after the deed was recorded, an attorney will start with those sections.

sections.h2: When a TOD deed is the wrong tool
sections.html:
It fits best with a single parcel and one clear beneficiary. It fits poorly when several heirs may disagree, when the home carries heavy debt, or when the owner wants a trust to manage the property.

  • A beneficiary who dies before the owner brings in the survival and substitution rules in sections 20 and 22.
  • Co-owners can undo the intended result by how they hold title.
  • The deed does not remove debts from the property.

An estate planning attorney can compare a TOD deed with a trust or a will for your situation. This page is general information and is not legal advice.

faqs.q: Does an Indiana TOD deed avoid probate?
faqs.a: For the parcel it covers, yes. The beneficiary takes title through the recorded deed. Other assets in the estate can still need probate.

faqs.q: Where do you record an Indiana TOD deed?
faqs.a: With the recorder of deeds in the county where the real estate is located, before the owner's death. A deed recorded after death is void.

faqs.q: Can I cancel a TOD deed by writing a new will?
faqs.a: No. A will or trust cannot revoke or modify a TOD deed. The owner must record a new deed or an acknowledged affidavit before death.

faqs.q: Can the beneficiary stop me from selling my house?
faqs.a: No. While the owner is alive, a beneficiary has no rights in the property because of the designation. A sale during life ends the designation for that parcel.

faqs.q: Does the beneficiary have to pay my mortgage?
faqs.a: The beneficiary takes the house subject to existing liens and security interests. The loan stays attached to the property, and lenders keep their rights.
